speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have no desire to speak at any length on the second reading of this bill. I take it that in committee there will be opportunity for all of us to go into the bill section by section. Consequently there is no particular reason why any time should be taken up at the second reading stage of the legislation.

While I do not think we should spend much time in discussing this bill npw, because its subject matter has been thoroughly considered during the debate on the resolutions, I am glad to note that something is to be done for the merchant seamen and the men in the ferry command.
I wish to make a plea for reconsideration of regulations which may have been made under the act. At this time I intend to raise one point, and deal with it briefly. I have a communication from a lady in which she draws to my attention a circumstance in connection with our income tax regulations which seems to me to be unfair. I place the following facts before the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson). For obvious reasons I shall not give the name of the person involved. The woman states:
I claimed exemption on my income tax return for the support of an illegitimate daughter and was advised by the inspector of income tax . . .
At a point in Ontario.
. . . that such an exemption could not be allowed, due to the fact that the child was [Mr. Graydon.l
illegitimate and therefore no blood relative of mine. He suggested adoption, claiming that this would legalize the relationship, and then they would be able to grant me the allowance for a dependent.
She goes on to say:
I have been the sole support of this child since her birth. I have established her in a respectable home, properly feed and clothe her, and am having her taught music. . . .
I have thoroughly investigated the possibility of an adoption and have been advised by the children's aid society that they will not make representations for such adoption, as they claim she is my dependent as it now stands, and adoption would be absurd. They believe that the income tax department will eventually be forced to recognize the injustice of the ruling they have made. As it now stands I cannot adopt the child without the representation of the children's aid society, and am therefore left at the mercy of the income tax department.
I bring this to the attention of the minister so that the policy in regard to cases of this kind may be reconsidered. The fact that this is an illegitimate child means that the mother has had an exceedingly difficult time in maintaining it. She has brought it up respectably, has educated it and is giving it special training. This regulation seems to me to be simply a survival from the bad old days when punishment was meted out in such circumstances.
I present the facts at this time because I maj' be called out of the chamber later in the evening. I bring it to the attention of the minister because I feel that in such cases, where the mother continues to care for the child, instead of abandoning it to charity, as is done sometimes, proper recognition should be given. I suggest that this is a proper case for a change in departmental policy.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. W. G. GIBSON (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The point raised is not a matter of income tax regulation. The question has arisen on several occasions as to whether the parent of an illegitimate child should be granted an allowance. It has been referred to the Department of Justice, and we have been informed that under the wording of the act "child" means a legitimate child, and that under the circumstances we were not authorized by the act to grant exemptions in respect of illegitimate children.

May I add a word to what has been said by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). If, as the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson) has said, that is the ruling of the Department of Justice, we ought to get another name for justice, because certainly that is neither justice nor sense. A

Income War Tax
child is a child. As a matter of fact, in my opinion there are no illegitimate children. There may be illegitimate parents, but the children are not illegitimate. Therefore they should not be punished. This is a punishment on the child more than on the mother. If the mother has not sufficient income properly to rear the child, then the child as well as the mother will suffer. In this day and age it is disgraceful to have a ruling of this kind.

Mr. Speaker, may I follow up what has been said by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). Within the past couple of weeks I brought a case to the attention of the minister. A long time ago I came to the conclusion that the minister should have some latitude in matters of this kind. The case I brought to his attention is an even more glaring example of injustice, and indicates even more clearly the necessity for some latitude in the interpretation of the law in respect of claims of this kind.
The person whose claim I placed before the department had taken control of two children belonging to his sister. Her husband had died, and she had not sufficient income to maintain her family. The brother has been maintaining those children for five or six years. Certainly he does not wish to adopt them, because at some time the mother expects to reestablish her home. Nevertheless he is granted no exemption for those children. He has to pay his income tax, because it is assessed against him. He of course receives consideration for his wife and the one child of his own. He has made numerous applications to have the matter straightened out, but is told repeatedly that the children cannot be exempted, unless they are adopted. This man is placed in an awkward position. He does not wish to insist upon his sister's permitting him to adopt her children, and still she is not able to maintain them.
In matters of this kind I believe some common sense should be applied. Possibly we cannot enact a law which will take care of all problems which may arise, but in my view the minister should have sufficient latitude in his interpretation of the law to take care of cases of this kind.
Mr. R. W. -GLADSTONE (Wellington South):	Mr. Speaker, a case similar to the
one reported by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has come to my attention. This is the case of a mother who
for some fifteen years has maintained an illegitimate daughter, and has been refused any deductions on her income tax returns. This mother has maintained a home, paid taxes, paid for gas, water, light and heat, and in every waj has been maintaining a proper home for the daughter. However, she is not allowed any deductions in respect of her income tax on that account. It seems to me that in equity she is entitled to some consideration.

Mr. Speaker, before the matter is closed I should like to add my word to those of hon. members who have already spoken. Two or three sessions ago I spoke at some length with respect to this matter, when the question of exemptions for hosts of British guest children was before the house. While that matter has never been rectified in form, it has been more than rectified in spirit, in a way I shall not discuss at the moment.
However, at that time I put a question on the order paper asking how many foster children there were in the country, and was unable to get an answer because the census returns were not completed, and the Department of National Revenue had no information whatever as to how many dependent children there were in the country, who were not looked after by their parents. I do not know what loopholes the Department of National Revenue is up against in according decent treatment to people who look after these children, when the children are not their own. At that time I pointed out that if a mother should die leaving a child which was taken care of by a brother who for good reasons did not care to adopt the child, he would not receive exemption for the upkeep and care. Surely a man, or a woman for that matter, who undertakes an obligation such as that is entitled to an allowance for upkeep of the child, even more so than a parent.
I have never been able to find out from either the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson) or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) just why no consideration is given to these most worthy cases. I ask the Minister of National Revenue to give an answer to this question, because I contend that the person who takes care of a child is entitled to the usual income tax exemption. If there is some reason for not adopting the principle that every child should be the subject of income tax exemption, I should like to know what it is. We find that departments sometimes have reasons, or say they have reasons for not adopting certain suggestions which

Income War Tax
are made, but we are seldom given those reasons. I have come to the conclusion that very often the reasons do not exist apart from some slight administrative difficulty. I call upon the Minister of National Revenue to adduce the reasons why he is not willing to make every child in this country the subject of income tax exemption.

Mr. Speaker, may I take this opportunity to bring another case to the attention of the minister. I understand that when a child is attending an educational institution such as a collegiate, a university or a business college, the parent is entitled to an exemption under the provisions of the act of 1942. I am informed also that when a child is taking a nursing course in a hospital, receiving no salary, her father being responsible for her clothing and whatever else she may require, the parent is allowed no exemption. I wonder why the department has decided that the parent of a child attending business college or collegiate or university is entitled to an exemption, while the father of a girl taking a course of training in a hospital is not entitled to an exemption. Nursing is a very honourable profession, and instruction is essential. These girls are performing a splendid and much needed service at the present time. I should like to hear from the minister in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), but I should like to approach this problem from another angle. Generally speaking, we in Canada are in favour of keeping children in private homes rather than in public charitable institutions. An illegitimate child or any child kept in a private home is much better off than if he were in an institution. It would simply be common sense to hold out every inducement to foster parents to look after children in their homes by their firesides rather than to penalize the parents by not granting income tax exemptions. This refusal may force them to place the children in a hospital, a nursing home or an institution where they may become charges on the community. Apart altogether from the benefit to the child itself; apart altogether from the benefit to the foster parent, or guardian, there is the great benefit to the community through- having these children properly cared for.. We should do eveo'thing possible to encourage the care of children by guardians or foster parents. Our juvenile court records reflect in no uncertain terms the disadvantages of not having children
fMr. Jackman ]
cared for by foster parents or guardians. I wish to add my voice to urge that these foster parents and guardians be given every inducement to keep children in their care.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Bradette in the chair.
On section 1-Annuities.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would the minister give [DOT] us some explanation of this particular section, because it contains some contentious provisions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The story is a long one but I shall try to make it as short as possible. Section 3 of the Income War Tax Act provides for the taxation of annuities or other annual payments, and it provides for it under two divisions of subsection 1. Section 3, subsection 1 (b), provides for the taxation of annuities or other annual payments received under the provisions of any contract except as in this act otherwise provided; and section 3, subsection 1 (g) provides for the taxation of annuities or other annual payments received under the provisions of any will or trust, irrespective of the date on which such will or trust became effective, and notwithstanding that the annuity or annual payment was in whole or in part paid out of capital funds of the estate or trust, and whether the same is received in periods longer or shorter than one year. From time to time representations have been made that we should alter our law in such a way that annuities or other annual payments would not be wholly included in income for taxation purposes. The argument which has been advanced is this, that when a person receives an annuity he is receiving yearly payments which are partly a return of capital, or part capital and part interest. We have followed the law of Great Britain in our treatment of annuities. The statute law of Great Britain makes all annuities and other annual payments taxable, whether they are contractual annuities or whether they are annuities payable under a will or trust. There are, however, decisions which define annual payments, and apparently the natural or dictionary meaning of "annual payments" is not the meaning given to that expression by the British decisions. Annual payments are treated by those decisions as equivalent to annuities, as another name for annuities, and annuities do not include what we call term annuities, annuities payable for a period of years certain, but annuities which last until the death of the

Income War Tax
annuitant or at least in some way depend for their termination date upon the death of the annuitant.
In this country there was a different wording of this section prior to 1938. As I have stated, we attempted to apply the law to annuities or other annual payments received under the provisions of any will or trust, although the wording of this section 3, subsection 1 (g) was not the same before 1938 as it is now. A case was taken to the courts which, I understand, was on the point, and the crown lost it. The section was then amended so as to take the present form of section 3, subsection 1 (g). However, the state of the law was not very well understood, and perhaps is not up to this date; representations have been made that there has been much hardship to those who receive annuities or other annual payments under wills, notably widows; and one of the trust companies circulated a booklet setting out certain cases of hardship. The hardship arises from the joint impact of succession duties and income taxation.

If I may refer to the same booklet as I believe the minister has, in one case, that of a $50,000 bequest, $50,300 was eaten up in succession duties and income taxes; but in the other case which they mentioned, I believe the estate was eaten up, not chiefly because of succession duties, but rather because of the effect of income tax where the widow was allowed under the terms of the will to supplement her income up to a stated figure by drawing on the capital of the estate; the capital she drew was added to her own income, and the tax rate was such an effectively high rate that virtually none of the capital accrued to the benefit of the widow; all of it went in taxation. Whereas, as the minister has said, most of these difficulties have arisen through both succession duties and income tax, they can at the same time arise through the operation of income tax alone. Is that not so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I will proceed with . my statement.

Well, is that so? Am I right, or am I not? It is not succession duties; it is income tax alone, the incidence of which can be so severe, if you are going to treat principal as income, that it is possible under certain draftsmanship contained in wills already existing, and perhaps under draftsmanship in wills to be drawn in the future unlesis solicitors are well aware of the terms of the law, that a great deal of principal will be treated as income and very little of the principal will find its way for the
purpose intended,, nameljq the upkeep of the family after the decease of the husband and father.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; it would be possible, even if there were no succession duty at all, for a will to be drawn in such a way that there would be considerable hardship. To my mind that would be possible only if the testator underestimated very seriously the value of his estate, because if he left a true annuity to his wife, and there was sufficient either by way of capital or interest to yield an annuity fo the lifetime of the widow, it would not. I think, be a hardship for the widow to pay income tax on these annual payments during her life as if they were income. They are in fact income; that is, they have been defined as income under the British legislation, and they are defined as income in our legislation. The testator has in that case converted his capital into income; he has left his wife an income for life; and that income is taxable as income, both in Great Britain and here. The hardship arises where the testator has underestimated very considerably the size of his estate, and that may have arisen from the fact that he did not expect such heavy succession duties as have in fact been imposed.
But the hon. gentleman is right. The heavy succession duties are not absolutely necessary. They are not a condition precedent to the underestimate o| the quantum of the estate. He may have underestimated for other reasons. If I leave my wife $3,000 per annum for life, and there is not enough to last her for more than three years and she lives for thirty years and pays income tax on the $3,000 at full rates for those three years, I would call that a hardship. That is what I am talking about. But if there were enough to last her for thirty years, as I expected there would be, even though it used up the entire estate I would not consider that there was any hardship in the income tax being payable on that. Opinions may differ on this. I am approaching the question from this point of view, that annuities are income; they are not a return of capital. I am basing that on the British cases. Case after case affirms the principle that when I buy an annuity, even though it costs me $25,000, and even though I have nothing left when I die, the annuity which I have received during those years is income. The capital is gone. It has lost its identity as capital. It has lost its character and quality as capital. It has been transformed from capital to income.

Income War Tax

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would there not be two income taxes on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Because he pays income tax on the money which he accumulates for the purpose of buying the annuity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Right.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Then, when he is paid the annuity he pays income tax again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he bought it out of capital, that would not be true. But the point is immaterial, it seems to me. One does not go back to the source of the money. If I had the cases here I could read them. The language of the Lords' decision is striking. There is no doubt at all what the law is in Britain, or in Australia and in the other British dominions. I am not prepared to depart from that principle in Canada, at least in time of war. It is fair to say that the United States have a different principle. The United States have worked out a plan of taxing a certain income element in the annuity. But the United States tax capital gains.
And allow capital losses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not hear my bon. friend. If he will rise in his place I will answer him.

I cannot see why we cannot frame our own tax laws without regard to Britain or the United States. The minister has just said that Britain taxes all annuity payments as if they were entirely income. The United States differentiates, as every sound accountant would differentiate, as between principal and income in regard to annuity payments. A certain part of annuity payments is income and a certain part is principal. That is easily ascertainable by an accountant. The minister says that in the United States they tax capital gains and I interjected that they also allow for capital losses. But the United States is not necessarily right, nor is Great. Britain. We in Canada must be allowed to think for ourselves in relation to our own affairs without necessarily borrowing from Great Britain or the United States. But what happens as a rule is that the crown takes from a particular country what best suits its own tax purposes, and that is why Canadians are the most heavily taxed people in the world to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are not.

I would think that corporations undoubtedly are more heavily taxed 
in Canada than in Great Britain, and our personal income tax rates are much higher than Britain's. If the minister wishes to deny that statement, all right, but I will stick to my guns in that regard. The total taxation in this country is extremely high; I do not know of any country where it is as high on a great many of our people.
With regard to these annuities it would seem as though the minister is going to be adamant in his refusal to separate that part of the annuity which is principal from that part which is income. Then it would be wholly unwise for any Canadian citizen ever to provide himself or his dependents with an annuity. It would be a most unsound type of investment particularly with the high income tax rates which we have in this country, and even if they are lowered in the future they will still be fairly high. If the minister persists in adopting that attitude, it means that he will exclude the purchase of annuities from every citizen in this country who is endeavouring to provide for his own old age and social security by that means of subsistence. As I understand it, at the present time if a husband leaves to his widow the income from a fund of $50,000, we will say, and if he gives the widow the right to draw on the principal of the fund in order to meet any emergency expenses, such as the education of the children, sickness, or operations, or anything else which the widow may choose; suppose she has the right to draw up to $5,000 in any year, as I understand it the whole $5,000 is taxable as income to the widow, even though the $50,000 is invested in government bonds at three per cent, which would yield only $1,500. Nevertheless, whether the widow takes the money or not, she is subject to a tax on $5,000, and if she happens to be young and have a family of tender years, the total capital will soon be dissipated. If, on the other hand, the husband has been provident enough to go to a good solicitor who understands taxation measures and spends probably all his time in endeavouring to keep up with the law, the will may be so drawn that the executors other than the widow would have the right to give her up to $5,000, in which case, although it is exactly the same money, that additional money making up the $5,000 per annum is not taxable. The minister will correct me if I am wrong. Therefore it is merely a question whether a person has been well advised legally in the drafting of a testamentary document. Surely the minister is not going to make it difficult and put an undue burden on people who have not consulted expert lawyers.

Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It appeared to me that the
first thing to decide was whether we should adopt the principle urged by the hon. gentleman. If we adopt that principle for annuities under wills as a principle of our taxation system, it would appear to me that the argument would be very strong for adopting it for contractual annuities as well. Otherwise, situations would arise where there would be discrimination. For instance, one man provides in his will that his executors shall buy an annuity for his widow from an insurance company. That being a contractual annuity, would be taxable. If he directed his executors to pay his wife an annuity out of the estate, that annuity would be taxable only to the extent of income. It would be urged at once that we would have to treat both of those annuities in the same way. Consequently it would appear to me that there is a fundamental principle at stake here, namely whether to adopt the United States system or stick to the British system. The hon. gentleman is quite right in saying that, in deciding, we should not be guided by the fact that it is the United States or the British system, but by what is the correct principle. The lenient principle, the easiest for the taxpayer, is to adopt the hon. gentleman's suggestion and free a large part of these annuities from taxation. But personally I do not think the consequences the hon. gentleman predicts as likely to follow from continuing to do what we have done in the past and what a good many other countries which I have named do, will follow. I think persons will buy annuities and will recognize the fact that those annuities do constitute income, and will be prepared to pay tax on that income. It may be that some will say they will not buy annuities; they will invest the money, they will buy bonds or shares or something like that and just pay income tax on the interest. Then they run many risks, and they have a smaller return themselves during their lifetime. Speaking for myself, I have a government annuity- although that is nobody's concern-but I certainly expect to pay income tax on that government annuity; it appears to me its true nature is income.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister has
educated himself to think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps so. I get so many
hundred dollars a year, beginning at a certain date, until the day I die. I regard that as income; it is irrelevant whether the purchase price of that annuity came out of some capital I had or some income; I have exchanged my capital; the purchase price is gone, and instead I have an income.
As far as my recommendations go I am going to stick to the taxation of these incomes. I do not see any basis for departing from it, particularly at a time like this. To depart from it would be to introduce a most drastic change into our income tax system. If you were to place it before the house without any influence from the government, I do not think hon. members would say to-day that it should be done-; that is, unless they just went on the principle that the fewer and lighter the taxes, the better.

Is there not another aspect that we should look at, particularly in these days when we are figuring on unemployment insurance and all sorts of plans to give the individual a feeling of security? Should we not in framing our taxation structure frame it as a means of encouraging the purchase of government annuities, particularly by those in the lower brackets? Should not a government annuity if purchased by a life annuitant or left by a will have an exemption up to a certain figure? Annuities sold through the Department of Labour as fostered by the government have set limits whereby a person can buy only an annuity which pays a stipulated amount, and that limitation is very low as far as accumulation or retention of capital is concerned. In this age when public opinion is seeking more security I think the minister would be well advised to take into consideration this aspect, as a means of encouraging the independence and security that one seeks when one buys or leaves an annuity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I hear the hon. gentleman, but I am not sympathetic with his point of view. I regard the annuities as income, and. as far as my recommendations go will continue so to regard them. What we have here confirms that principle. All contractual annuities are untouched, and annuities under wills and trusts which become effective after January 1, 1944, are to be subject in the future to the same rule that has applied to them in the past. I wish to make that clear and definite and public, because I do not want misunderstandings about this matter that have existed in the past to continue. There is a period during which there is a case for relief. It is a question as to how far that relief should be extended, what the time limit of it should be. But it seems to me that with regard to wills of testators who died before 1938 and who. therefore, could not change their wills to comply with our amendment of 1938, there is a case for relief. And as the hon. gentleman has said, there has been a difference in the treatment that persons receiving payments under wills have received. I do not mean that the treatment by taxation authorities
Income War Tax

has been different, but some persons have been better advised than others; solicitors who were skilful in the matter have been able to advise them how to draw their wills so that some have escaped because the annual payments have not been true annuities, and some not so well advised have not escaped because the payments are true annuities. This section states that vith regard to any wills and trusts which became effective prior to January 1, 1944, the Income beginning with the income of the taxation year 1943 will be exempt from income tax to the extent that they are paid out of capital, but only up to SI,500 a year. That will give some relief to a limited class; it will give them an opportunity to order their affairs in another way, if they wish to do so, before January 1, 1944. If they do so, we have no complaint, but we certainly do not want to whittle away and shatter this principle because, it is a principle of the greatest importance.

I do not understand the distinction the minister made between a contractual annuity and an annuity, I presume, under a will or trust. He suggested that there was some difference in the method of taxation. Certainly, as far as anything I have put forward in the way of suggestions for equitable taxation is concerned, I have not had in mind any distinction between a contractual annuity and an annuity under a will or trust.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is exactly what I said. I said that if we were to change this rule, as we have been strongly urged to do, so that annuities payable under wills are to be freed to the extent that they are paid out of capital, and do nothing more, we would have just started on a bigger problem. I do not think we can stop there. Consequently after giving the matter very careful consideration, I decided not to depart from that principle-that is, the principle of taxing them as income-but to affirm that principle and to give limited relief for a certain period, due to the inequities that have arisen as a result of testators having died before the decision to amend the law. Then, for the period after that, for testators not knowing exactly what to do, with some making their wills in one way and being caught and others making them in another way and not being caught, we are giving them a time limit, to January 1, 1944. The relief will be granted to this limited extent for the wills and trusts that become effective before January 1, 1944, and after that there will be no relief. That is what it means.

As I understand this new clause, which we have seen for the first time
[Mr. Itsley.l
to-night, it seems to me that it would be very unwise financially for anyone to take out a contractual annuity, if the whole proceeds of that annuity are to be subject to taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They alw'ays have been.
Of course there have been a great number of annuities where there has been a certain amount of exemption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am wrong when I say they always have been. There was an exemption of government annuities for some years up to a certain amount, but the contractual annuities bought from insurance companies have always been taxable. There is no doubt about that.

I still believe there is a great inequity, resulting from the attitude taken by the Minister of Finance in regard to these annuities, which works a hardship on a great many of our people, in fact on nearly every person who leaves anything in the form of an annuity or who purchases an annuity with a stated income. When a man purchases an annuity,' let us say for $20,000, it is known definitely, when the price of that annuity is figured out exactly, how much of it is income which accrues from year to year and how much of it is principal. When the beneficiary dies, of course the whole annuity is exhausted. I have not looked at any of the English cases, because it seemed to me the matter was fairly simple from both an actuarial and an equitable point of view, but I realize perhaps something of what the minister has in mind when he says that when an annuity is purchased it is the transference of a capital sum for an annual flow. So far as the individual is concerned, that may be quite, so. When a person takes out an annuity he does in effect make a bet. He makes a wager that he may live longer than the amount of income which he would receive from the capital sum plus an annual drain on the capital, and at the same time he is insured as to a certain amount of annual revenue for life. Therefore there may be a slight uncertainty in regard to each individual annuity. But if we take annuities as a class, so far as the government is concerned-and it is interested in all the annuities held by people in Canada-there is no uncertainty whatsoever. The government knows or can readily determine how much of each annuity is income and how much is capital; and if it wishes to legislate fairly and to make its taxes bear equitably upon the people, it will tax only that part of an annuity payment which is income and not that part which is capital.
If we take the average of annuities, which again is what the government is interested in and how it is actually affected, it cannot

Income War Tax
possibly be the loser. But because a man wishes to make sure that his widow will have an annuity of $1,200 or $2,000 for life, the government says that the whole capital will be taxed. To show how improvident such a proposal is, I can only say that these annuities are based on a rate of three per cent, or perhaps 34 per cent. We all know that to have a safe annuity the company which issues it has to invest the money in government bonds; it has to pay the commissions of its * salesmen, its head office expenses and so on, and if it uses a base higher than three per cent it is not perhaps the type of company in which I would care to have an annuity. Consequently one is reduced to the point that a husband may just as well buy government bonds and leave them to his widow, who will get three per cent on them. If that is not enough to maintain her at a decent standard of living, then she will sell a bond or two each year and in that way maintain her standard. The difficulty so far as the government is concerned, and why the government should treat this matter fairly, is that the husband does not know how long his widow may live after he dies. He may leave a certain sum of money, figuring that if the widow draws three per cent on the principal and encroaches on the capital at the rate of $1,000 a year, she will have enough to take care of herself for twenty or twenty-five years. But the widow may be long-lived; she may live for thirty-five or forty years, in which case, she may have nothing left at the end of twenty-five years. When that comes to an average, however, the insurance companies give you a rate based on the average, and the government could just as easily take that average rate, because all the people in Canada come under the government and must pay taxes to it.
I will not say I am not concerned with the English decisions mentioned by the minister. I suppose I should read some of them to find out just what the learned law lords have said about this matter. But England is a country which is still reminiscent of the feudal system; where an individual may own a whole town; where leases fall due at the end of ninety-nine years or nine hundred and ninety-nine years; where coal mines are owned by people whose ancestors came over with William the Conqueror, and I am not greatly concerned with the application of such principles of law to a young and growing country like Canada. Surely we should be able to discover for ourselves the basis of sound principles of income tax law. Any accountant can tell you how much of any annuity is principal and
how much is income, and surely if the government wants to tax people fairly it should tax that part of an annuity which is income and leave free of income tax that part which is capital.

I do not know whether other hon. members are as confused as I am. after listening to the hon. member for Rose-dale and the Minister of Finance, but I am going to try to get a little enlightenment. At one time I thought I agreed with the Minister of Finance, but I believe now I agree with the hon. member for Rosedale. Do I understand that if a person invested $12,000 in an annuity and on reaching the age of sixty-five he withdraws that amount at the rate of $100 a month, that $100 a month is taxable as income?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

And do I understand that if, instead of buying an annuity, a person deposited a certain sum of money in the bank each month so that at the age of sixty-five he had $12,000 in the bank, he could draw out that money at the rate of $100 a month and it would not be taxable as income?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, but it might not last as long as he lived.
What is the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The money might run out.
The other might run out too, as the hon. member for Rosedale has said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; it cannot possibly run out; that is the difference. The first case is the return of capital; the second is a purchase of an income for life. The life element is what makes the difference.
There was a considerable capital investment, though.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is true, but the individual exchanged his capital for income.

Since the minister has
conceded a certain amount of the principle in this section, and if it is sound, why does he limit it to not exceeding $1,500 in any year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Because it is a measure to
relieve the hardest cases; that is all.

The minister does not
concede the principle?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; I do not concede the
principle at all.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
Income War Tax

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On section 3-Dividends received by one corporation from another.

Is this the section which changes section 4 (n) in the old act? I note the marginal heading is, "dividends received by one corporation from another," and paragraph (n) reads:
Dividends paid to an incorporated company by a company incorporated in Canada, the profits of which have been taxed under this act, except as hereinafter provided by sections 19, 22A and 32A.
Does this mean that dividends from one Canadian company to another Canadian company are now to be taxable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The only change is the
addition of 32A. The hon. member will recall that under the amended section 32A there is a case where dividends may be taxable in the hands of the company receiving them. That is, of course, after this treasury board procedure, finding, and so on. The hon. member protested against it the other night. I would point out again that the only addition is that of 32A. The other sections are already in the act.

This is not the main
section respecting the amendment in the Income War Tax Act in connection with section 32 A.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-Service pay and allowances.

The last words in the section refer to the matter about which some of us were speaking the other night, namely the Royal Air Force transport command, formerly known as the ferry command. This does not give, of course, everything that was asked on behalf of these men. However, while I have not been able to get in touch with their views, because the bill is only just now before us, on looking at it from an unprejudiced point of view I think the suggested arrangement is a reasonable one. Therefore, on behalf of the men I take it upon myself to express their appreciation.
There is one point, however, I should like the minister to dwell upon. This matter was discussed before, I believe, and has to do with the cost of living at Nassau. I am told it is nearly double what it is in Canada. I admit we cannot very well adjust a condition like that through an income tax bill, but perhaps the minister would pass the word along, or indicate in what way some maintenance allowance might be given to the men sent to those places. I believe such allowances are given

to civil servants who are sent to the Yukon, where the cost of living is much higher than elsewhere in Canada.
On the general principle of taxation, however, I am glad to express appreciation for the consideration the minister has given the matters presented to him, but I would point out that this cost of living does fall heavily on the people who go to Nassau. It may be urged that they do not go there often, but a man may be there for a year. I am informed there is no price fixing or rental fixing. Perhaps the minister would undertake to pass the word along.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall make a note of what the hon. member has said, and bear it in mind, but I do not think it will do much good, because we are not the employers. The British government are the employers, and the pay is pretty substantial.

It seems to me that the exemptions provided for members of his majesty's forces returning from overseas do not go very far, compared with those offered in the British budget. The man returning from overseas may not be able to get a house. I say he should be allowed at least one year's exemption, because he is still on active service. He is wearing a uniform, and has been paid an allowance by the government, on both a per diem and a subsistence basis. I say he is still on active service for one year. I can see no reason why members of our armed forces, who have been tied up in England for about four years, upon their return to Canada should not be allowed one year's exemption from income tax.
The section makes reference to the exemption of war risk bonus of members of the merchant marine. I say the merchant marine has been the backbone of our fleet. For many years it has been the backbone of our navy, including the corvettes, and the boats of other types we have heard described.
The ferry command has been doing a fine piece of work, and I would urge the minister to reconsider the matter, and give increased allowances to these men.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not wish to speak at length respecting the merchant navy or the Royal Air Force transport command. However, I was greatly impressed by certain evidence placed before the committee by hon. members to my left, as well as by a statement by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services. Some of the information placed before the committee when the resolutions were under discussion indicated that what the minister said about the differentiation between

Income War Tax
civilians and those in the armed forces indicated that he was hanging his argument on a pretty slim thread, so far as members of the merchant navy were concerned. The Minister of National Defence for Naval Services said that they had guns on their boats, and that they did not shoot one way but shot the other. He indicated that their operations were entirely defensive. I thought that was carrying the argument a little too far. I could not very well see what difference it made to a man in the hold of a merchant vessel whether he shot a gun at someone who had already attacked him, or whether he fired the first shot. I cannot see myself how that makes any difference. However, the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services seemed to make a point of it, and the Minister of Finance said that he wanted to keep in force the distinction between members of the armed forces and civilians.
I am not an expert on naval matters, but looking at this from an unbiased point of view-I think most hon. members will do likewise-I should be inclined to think that under present conditions there would be more danger for the man in the merchant marine than there is for the man on a firsGclass cruiser or corvette or some other vessel of that kind which is well able to take care of itself. I cannot imagine any worse place for a man to be in than in a semi-protected vessel which, as the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services says, has a gun to be used for defence only. I can think of a man in the hold of such a ship and always having the fear in his mind that something will come through the side of the ship. I have great difficulty in seeing how the minister can draw such a fine line between the civilian on a ship which is in such danger that it must be armed, and the member of the armed forces.
I do not wish to make a lengthy argument out of this, but I do want the minister to know how I feel about it. It is unfortunate that no provision was made in the bill for those who serve on armed vessels, those who are actually engaged in the transporting of goods through the most dangerous parts of the Atlantic, those who must face the submarine menace. I cannot understand how those people should be regarded as ordinary civilians for the purpose of income tax or anything else. They are doing perhaps one of the most dangerous jobs in the whole war effort. I must say that we are thankful for small mercies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is not a small one.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Of course the minister's
mind works in devious channels. His idea of a large concession is what many of us might regard as a small one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman must
realize that this concession means that the overwhelming majority will not be taxable at all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This is not the first time that I have risen in my place to say that I have a great deal of difficulty in swallowing the idea that we should be taxing people who fight in order to pay others who fight.
I am not going to deal with that phase specially to-night because it is something I have spoken about on previous occasions, but to exempt only the bona fide war risk bonus which is, I think, something like $25 a month-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: $45 a month beyond coastal waters.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Make it $45; make it
as large as you like; there is still another $106 a month that is taxable from the ordinary seaman in the merchant navy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is not correct; it is
included.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Perhaps the minister
could tell me what is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the $106 includes
the $45.
Mr. GRAYDON; I am quite sure it does not. During the debate on the resolution $25 was mentioned as the amount being exempted and $106 as the amount that was still being taxed. I do not wish to weary the minister at this stage. He has made up his mind, and when he says "no" you can take it as "no". I have learned that through the years. Some concession has been made in connection with the transport command of the Royal Air Force, and one-third of the remuneration of these men is to be exempted. If the minister cannot see his way clear to amend this section dealing with the merchant marine, I ask him to consider changing the definition of civilian and member of the armed forces before he brings in another Income War Tax Act amendment.
The minister told the leader of the opposition that this concession will exempt the majority of the men in the merchant marine from the payment of income tax, but I do not think that is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would say ninety per cent. I can find out, but it is the overwhelming majority.
Income War Tax

I have a fair idea of the rates. The lowest rate is that paid to the AB, who receives $106 a month exclusive of war bonus. According to the information which I received only a few days ago the bonus to the AB is $25 a month,. The bonus varies according to income and the income varies according to classification of occupation. An, AB is exempt from payment on his war risk bonus which amounts to $25 a month, but he still pays a tax on the $106 a month. The majority of these men are single, and they would: be paying tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is the hon. member quoting those rates from memory, or does he have the figures before him?
I had them here the other "day, and I took the lowest rate because that is the one in which I was interested.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says that in the case of the AB the bonus is payable over and above the $106; is that right?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The figures I have were obtained from a company which is re,pre-sented as being a typical company. They give the following rates for an AB:
Basic rate	 $ 56 20
War risk bonus	 44 50
Cost-of-living bonus	 18 42
Total	 $119 12
The amount that would be taxable would be $119.12 less $44.50.
What company is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Park Steamship company.
Does the minister mean to tell me that men are crossing the ocean for a basic rate of $56?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the basic rate for an AB, but the total is $119.12.
Is the minister certain that that is not the inland rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is the war risk bonus over the coastal rate. There is no war risk bonus for inland waters, but the coastal rate is about $25.

I had the figures the other, day, but I only put the low rate on the record because if they get an exemption it would take care of those in the upper brackets as well. I secured my figures only last week from a man who has to do with the hiring and' firing of men, in the merchant marine.
I have never heard those rates before.
I wonder whether the rate mentioned by the hon. member for Cape Breton South is not the Canadian rate, whereas the rate mentioned by the minister is the British rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: He is discussing the deep-sea rates.
I think there must be some difference in the two. That is probably where the difference in the argument comes in. It seems to me like three pounds a week. It is about that sum, on the exchange.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The official who went into that is not here.

I should like to add a word to that given by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. As one of the members who was interested the other evening in trying to get some consideration for the young men in the ferry command, I am pleased that the minister took these representations into consideration and has gone as far as he has. I think some of us felt that nothing could be expected, that the minister's mind had been made up; and we all know, as the leader of the opposition said a few moments ago, that when the Minister of Finance makes up his mind-and we respect him for it-usually he sticks to what he says he is going to do. Consequently, even though this does not go as far as some hon. members hoped, I think it is a substantial concession, and I say this on behalf of my colleagues and myself. I am sure, too, that if he had an opportunity of asking the young men who made representations to the department their opinion of what has been done, they would express their thanks to the ' minister for having granted this concession.
So far as the merchant seamen are concerned, it might be well if the minister would look into the rates. I am quite satisfied that the rate he quoted is the British rate, much lower than the Canadian rate. There is no class of men engaged in active service in this war who are deserving of more consideration than the merchant seamen. We appreciate the risks which are taken by our men in the armed forces, especially, perhaps, in the air force; but the men who cross the seas in ships to-day-with what we know of the condition of the north Atlantic, particularly-are risking their lives all the time. I heard a statement of an authority a short time ago-I will not say who it was, but it was very high authority-that it is estimated that in recent months the loss in merchant seamen ran to something like a quarter of the crews torpedoed. If that is so, or if the casualty list approaches such a

Income War Tax
figure, it comes fairly close to the casualty lists we spoke of in connection with the ferry command; and to my mind any concessions we can make for the merchant seamen are fully justified.
I am glad that concessions to these two groups have been made. I express our appreciation, and I hope that further consideration will be given, and that these men, particularly those who go down to the sea in ships, will receive the concessions they deserve.

Is there anything in prospect for the widows and children of merchant seamen similar to the reparations which were paid to the families of merchant seamen sunk by enemy action, following the last war? I was on a reparations committee at that time, and many of the families received payments from that source. If there is nothing like that to-day, I too, wish to say a word for merchant seamen. Whether ocean-going ships are armed or unarmed makes no difference in this regard. The ship which is unarmed has that much less chance of getting through than the ship which is armed, and the sailors on board an unarmed ship as well as those on a merchant ship with one gun are always in jeopardy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot give the hon. gentleman any information about reparations. I do not know that I understand what the reparations would be.
German ships which were seized in port in the last war were afterwards sold, and the money received from the sales was distributed among the families of merchant seamen who lost their lives.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know whether there will be anything like that or not.

Having come in a little late, I asked for a copy of the bill, but there appear to be no more left. May I have a copy? It seems to me extraordinary, with so few hon. members in the house, that one is unable to get a copy of the bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the section carry?
No. I, too, would like a copy of the bill, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Section 5 agreed to.
On section 6-Farm losses.
This clause varies somewhat from the resolution which was passed, does it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think so.
I was under the impression, when we were on the resolution, that only losses for 1942 were deductible against future income of those engaged chiefly in farming.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The section at the end of the bill will make this subsection 1, paragraph (r) applicable to incomes for the year 1944. If the hon. gentleman will look at it he will see the effect of that:
(r) losses sustained in the process of earning income from the operation of any farm during the two years last preceding the taxation year-
That is 1944.
-by a person whose chief occupation is that of farming.
These losses can be brought forward against the profits of 1944. The hon. gentleman will ask, what about 1943? The existing'section, which is general in its application, allows losses to be brought forward one year; therefore the person can bring 1942 losses forward against the profits of 1943. That is provided for under the general section, but this specially applies to farms, and for the year 1944 and subsequent years.
Would 1943 be called the taxation year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, 1944 will be the taxation [DOT] year for the purposes of this section.
Then, for 1943 the farmer may not charge back two years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not two, no.
Well, that is the same as the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
That is what we had all the argument about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
I am sorry it does not apply to 1943.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have always been fairly insistent on the impossibility of ascertaining losses prior to 1942, when we started our legislation.
We are not going to reopen the argument to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

It seems to me there will be some difficulties in the mechanics of this section. Will the Minister of National Revenue explain how the farmer is to determine his actual losses? Is there a valuation of the farm at the beginning of the year and an inventory taken each year? How is the
23S0
Income War Tax

value of the farm to be determined? It seems to me it would be extremely variable and be affected by varying prices.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
The losses referred to are
not capital losses, but operating losses in the actual operation of the farm.

That is what I mean. How are the operating losses to be determined? Does the farmer take his income and his expenses? Is he allowed to take into account, in computing his cost of operation, the number of hours of horse labour and team labour?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The cost of maintenance of the horses would not be a charge because he would not be in the business of hiring horses.

In farm management the farmer works out the number of hours of labour his horses have done. That is taken into account in figuring the cost of producing his commodities. There is an account for horse labour.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That might be a convenient method of arriving at the cost of production or something like that, but it would not be the way to arrive at the farmer's profit or ' loss. He could not put a value upon the use of his horses.
What about his labour costs? How does the Department of National Revenue figure the cost of operating?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The wages he pays his hired men would be an operating cost, but he cannot charge for his own labour.
Can he charge for the labour of his family?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not unless he pays them.
If he pays them, can he charge that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not for his wife, but for the others he can.
If he pays anything to his son or daughter for work on the farm, he can charge that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
But if he does not, he cannot?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, and he would lose his son as a dependent, of course, if he paid him.
Is he allowed deductions for the purchase of seed and cattle?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes
What about the forms he has to fill out this year? Have they been printed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: No; we are waiting for the bill to pass. Then they will be prepared and issued.
Will they be different from those of last year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The simplified form will in most instances be available with some extra inserts for the farmer.
There is nothing in the legislation we are passing that would require any alteration in the form? It is rather difficult for us to discuss the legislation unless we have the form.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The legislation does not specify what sorts of forms are to be issued. The income tax branch prepares the forms. They are not included in the act, with the exception of rates which are printed on them.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 7-Proviso.
This is an extremely difficult section, and I wish the minister would deal with it so that hon. members may understand what the subject matter is about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This has been pretty well covered in the resolutions and in the budget speech, and I think the section is drafted in such a way as to carry out the intentions as expressed. I perhaps should point out that the first proviso is not limited to companies which are owned by a common interest. There was some expression in the resolution about a common interest, but the expression used here is a controlling interest, which is defined in a recent House of Lords' decision in such a way that it is possible to determine whether or not a person has a controlling interest in a company.
May we have that definition in substance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You mean, put it on Hansard?
Yes, in substance, and have it now for the purpose of discussing this section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think it is necessary. We all have a pretty good idea of when one company has a controlling interest in another company or when one shareholder has a controlling interest in a company.

That is not the type of answer the minister should give. You can have effective control with ten per cent if the

Income War Tax
rest of the stock is widely distributed, or otherwise fifty-one per cent gives you legal control. I think the minister should be definite. I do not wish to delay him; in fact,
I think we have cooperated to the utmost extent, but I should like to know what is meant by the word "controlling".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will see if I cannot get that decision and read some excerpts from it.
Is it effective or legal control?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is effective control.
Ten per cent would do the trick then. If the minister would be good enough to put the relevant parts on Hansard, if they are not too lengthy, it would be helpful.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All right. Apart from that point altogether, this proviso is designed to prevent more than 100 per cent of the cost of assets being written off by virtue of being passed from one interest to another under circumstances where one controls the other. That is the effect of the section. I do not think I need read it.
Resolution 11 is covered by the first paragraph and resolution 12 by the second? Is that the way it works?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; this is correct. There may be some slight modifications of the resolutions, but these sections are designed to put into legislative form those two resolutions. I think it is dangerous to provide that only 100 per cent can be written off. There will be circumstances in which more than 100 per cent will be written off; that is, in sales to perfectly independent purchasers. But that just cannot be avoided. This is designed to hold the write-off of depreciation down to 100 per cent where the seller controls the buyer or the buyer the seller.
That relates to the first paragraph only?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. Generally speaking, controlling interest would be majority interest, but I do not think it is limited to that. I will see what, the House of Lords' decision says.
The second proviso is about the depreciation on the sale of movable assets. That is designed to carry out resolution 12. Resolution 12 is descriptive and is shorter than the section. It reads:
That where immovable assets (not including equipment or machinery) in respect of which special or accelerated depreciation has been allowed, are subsequently sold at a price in excess of the residual undepreciated value, such
excess shall be applied to reduce proportionately in each year the special or accelerated depreciation previously allowed to the transferor; provided, however, that such taxpayer shall not be deprived of ordinary depreciation which but for the special depreciation would have been allow-ed as a deduction from income.
There is a further limitation in the section. The resolution is more harsh than the section in certain circumstances. The section is so drawn that if the vendor realizes more than 100 per cent of his cost, he is entitled to that capital gain.
Do I understand the minister to say that if the property is sold for an amount over the present depreciated book value, the vendor is entitled to his capital gain?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Would it be too much trouble for the minister to give an actual example of this very complicated section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am hesitant to put an example on the record without giving it more thought than I can at the moment. Two or three days ago I had this clearly in my mind, and it was quite obvious that every clause of this was necessary:
Provided further that in the case of the sale of immovable assets (not including machinery or equipment) in respect of which special depreciation has been allowed, the minister may revise the assessments of the vendor for the years when the special depreciation was allowed, by disallowing as a reduction a pro rata portion of the special depreciation allowed to the taxpayer in each of the said years, to the extent of the excess of the selling price over the depreciation cost of the said assets. . . .
Let me interpose there. That is substantially what the section does, if we stopped there. But it would not be fair to leave it there. From that excess selling price over the depreciated cost we must make deductions; we must deduct the amount of depreciation normally allowed on the said assets. And, secondly, we must deduct the excess, if any, of the selling price over the undepreciated cost of the said assets. If he bought it for $100 and sold for $110, he should not be deprived of the $10.
So that he is allowed that capital gain?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; that is the capital gain over the cost, but that is different from allowing the capital gain over the undepreciated cost.

That seems clear enough. How would the minister treat a case where the plant-because this has to do with plant, anything which is not movable-is sold and
Income War Tax

the new price has to do entirely with the fact that within a year or two after the cessation of war the earning power has been built up by some business manager going in there, perhaps putting in some extra working capital, so that the sale price with an established earning power bears little or no relation to the physical plant which was depreciated. You may have another plant across the way still lying idle on which the same depreciation operated during the war years. It comes back to the assertion I made at the time the resolution was under discussion, that industrialists are not interested in buying bricks and mortar, because we see idle factories that stay idle until you get a business to put into them. The only thing that creates value is earning power; bricks and mortar are essential; but because a man chooses a plant on this side of the road rather than on the other side, and, after making a good job for a period of years, getting things working and creating employment, then sells the plant at a profit, you are going to make him write back into the earnings of the company the extra depreciation allowed during the war years when the rate of taxation was eighty per cent under the Excess Profits Tax Act. It seems to me that the minister may find many cases which are extremely difficult to deal with.
Secondly, supposing after this war we run into a period of inflation, through no fault of our own, certainly not through the action of the Minister of Finance, and bricks and mortar become worth a great deal more than they were at the time they were being depreciated; surely the owner of those bricks and mortar is entitled to the present value, which is not related to the cost or cost less depreciation, whether it be excessive depreciation or normal depreciation. British American Tobacco Co., Ltd. v. Inland Revenue Commissioners
[House of Lords (Viscount Simon, L.C., Lord Atkin, Lord Thankerton, Lord Russell of Killowen, Lord Porter), December 7, 8, 9, 1942]
Revenue-National defence contribution-"Controlling interest" in company-Indirect control
-Finance Act, 1937 (c. 54), Sched. IV, paras.
4, 7 (b), 11.
The appellant company held shares in 11 companies operating outside the United Kingdom, which were not, therefore, liable to he assessed to national defence contribution. In the case of 4 of these companies, the appellant company itself controlled more than 50 per cent of the votes. In the case of the remaining 7 companies, more than 50 per cent of the votes were controlled by the appellant company in conjunction with a company or companies in which the appellant company controlled more than 50 per cent of the votes:-
Held: the appellant company had a controlling interest in all the companies within the meaning of the Finance Act, 1937, Sched. IV, para. 7 (b), and the dividends received by the appellant company from these companies should be included in its income liable to national defence contribution.
Decision of the Court of Appeal ([1941] 2 All E.R. 651) affirmed.
[Editorial Note.-It has been unsuccessfully contended that a control by a bare majority holding is insufficient. The argument was that, to have a controlling interest, a controlling company must have such a holding that it could ensure the passing of resolutions which must be passed by more than a bare majority of votes. This contention has been rejected by all the courts and in a few sentences Viscount Simon, L.C., has shown that a bare majority of votes is sufficient for effective control of a company.
As to Control of Company, see Halsbury, Hailsham Edn., Vol. 17, pp. 89-92, para. 187, p. 290, para. 576; and for Cases, see Digest, Vol. 28, pp. 25-30, Nos. 136-154.]
Case referred to:
(1) Noble v. Inland Revenue Comrs. (1926), 12 Tax Cas. 911.
Appeal by the taxpayer from an order of the Court of Appeal, dated June 30. 1941, and reported [1941] 2 All E.R. 651, dismissing an
appeal from a decision of Lawrence, J., dated Apr. 8, 1941, and reported [1941] 2 All E.R. 86, where the facts are fully set out.
J. Millard Tucker, K.C., and John S. Scrimgeour for the appellants.
The Attorney-General (Sir Donald Somervell, K.C.), J. H. Stamp and Reginald P. Hills for the respondents.
Viscount Simon, L.C.: My Lords, this appeal is brought, by special leave of this House, from the order of the Court of Appeal (Scott, Clauson and Goddard, L.JJ.), which dismissed an appeal by the appellants from a judgment of Lawrence, J., on a case stated by the commissioners for special purposes of the Income Tax Acts. The matter arises upon an assessment to national defence contribution made upon the appellant company under the Finance Act, 1937, Part III, and the question in dispute is whether the appellant company had "a controlling interest" in certain foreign companies referred to in the case within the meaning of that expression as contained in the Finance Act, 1937, Sched. IV.
7 (b), so as to require that dividends received by the appellant company from these foreign companies should be included in its income liable to national defence contribution.
Counsel for the appellant company put forward two contentions in support of the view that the appellant company had no such controlling interest. First, he argued that "interest" in this connection means interest of a proprietary nature and that tjie condition that there should be a controlling interest would only be satisfied if the appellant company itself owned a sufficient shareholding in the other company to control the latter. Secondly, he contended that, in any event, a controlling interest is not constituted by the control of the bare majority of shares (whether directly or through other companies), but that the control must be of such proportion of shares as -would secure the passing of a special resolution or other resolution for which a special majority ' is required by the terms of the constitution of the foreign company.
These two contentions have been rejected as unsound by each tribunal which in turn has dealt with the appellant company's claim, and at each stage the decision arrived at has been in favour of the crown. Notwithstanding the full and careful argument addressed to the House. I take the view that the decision arrived at below was correct, and I understand that your Lordships are in agreement with me that the appeal should be dismissed.
The case turns on the meaning of the -words "controlling interest" in the context in which they are used. The appellant argues that, in order that one company should have a controlling interest in another, it must be the beneficial owner of a requisite number of shares in that other company, either registered in its own name or in the name of its nominees; and that if company No 1 owrns all the shares in company No. 2, which in turn owns all the shares in company No. 3, company No. 1 has no interest, controlling or otherwise, in company No. 3.
It is true that in such circumstances company No. 1 owns none of the assets of company No. 2, and a fortiori owns none of the assets of company No. 3, and in that sense neither owns, nor has an interest in, company No. 3. But that is to treat the phrase "controlling interest" as capable of connoting only a proprietary right, that is, an interest in the nature of ownership.
